'''Igor Vyacheslavovich Sutyagin''' ({{langx|ru|И́горь Вячесла́вович Сутя́гин}}; born 17 January 1965) is a Russian arms control and [[nuclear weapon]]s specialist. In 1998, he became the head of the subdivision for Military-Technical and Military-Economic Policy at the [[Institute for US and Canadian Studies]] of the [[Russian Academy of Sciences]] in [[Moscow]], where he worked before he was arrested for [[treason]] on accusations he had given information to a British company, although he had no access to classified documentation as a civilian researcher.<ref name="takeover">[https://dx.doi.org/10.1080/08850600500483699 The Chekist Takeover of the Russian State], Anderson, Julie (2006), International Journal of Intelligence and Counter-Intelligence, 19:2, 237 - 288.</ref> Sutyagin spent 11 years in prison on espionage charges and was released by Russia in 2010 in exchange for the release of [[Illegals Program|a group of spies]] arrested in the United States.

As of 2018, Sutyagin is a Research Fellow at the [[Royal United Services Institute for Defence and Security Studies]] in London.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nonproliferation.eu/thinktanks/thinktanks.php?tid=rusi|title=The EU Non-Proliferation Consortium - The Network|website=www.nonproliferation.eu|access-date=2 March 2014|archive-date=7 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180307082230/http://www.nonproliferation.eu/thinktanks/thinktanks.php?tid=rusi|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>[https://www.ft.com/content/938ce33e-a227-11e3-a621-00144feab7de Russian troops stick to a tried and tested script], 2 March 2014</ref><ref name="BBC-43303651">{{cite web|title=Boris Johnson warns Russia over spy collapse|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-43303651|website=BBC News|accessdate=6 March 2018|date=6 March 2018}}</ref>

==Background and trial==
With a degree in [[physics]] as well as [[history]], Sutyagin worked on topics relating to U.S. and Russian [[nuclear weapon]]s development, deployment and control and he is a co-author of a book on the [[Strategic Rocket Forces|Russian strategic nuclear forces]].<ref>This web page was removed. [http://russianforces.org/book/  Russian strategic nuclear forces]</ref>

In October 1999, the [[FSB (Russia)|Russian Federal Security Service]] detained Sutyagin and brought charges of [[espionage]] against him. They alleged that Sutyagin passed classified information to a London-based firm, [[Alternative Futures]]. Sutyagin acknowledged working with the company, but he said that all information about nuclear submarines he disclosed was based on material in the open literature and that, not having a security clearance, he never had access to classified sources.

In 2004, after a trial, a [[jury]] in Moscow unanimously found Sutyagin guilty of espionage. The jury found that Sutyagin disclosed secret information to [[Defense Intelligence Agency]] officers [[Shaun Kidd]] and [[Nadya Lokk]], and that Sutyagin was paid for this. The court sentenced Sutyagin to 15 years of imprisonment.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://txt.newsru.com/russia/14apr2004/igor.html|title=Приговор Игорю Сутягину, осужденному на 15 лет, обжалован в Верховном суде РФ|date=2004-04-14}}</ref> In December 2005 Sutyagin was transferred to a penal colony in [[Kholmogory, Arkhangelsk Oblast|Kholmogory]] near [[Arkhangelsk]].<ref name =release/>

==Reactions==
Sutyagin was listed as a [[political prisoner]] by [[Human Rights Watch]] and [[Amnesty International]].<ref>[http://web.amnesty.org/aidoc/ai.nsf/afec99eadc40eff880256e8f0060197c/80256dd400782b8480256ea600547604/$FILE/joint%20statement%20on%20the%20case%20of%20Igor%20Sutiagin%20-%20June%202004.rtf]{{Dead link|date=September 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} [https://2001-2009.state.gov/g/drl/rls/hrrpt/2005/61671.htm].</ref> Human Rights Watch stated that "the FSB showed little respect for Sutiagin’s [[right to a fair trial]]: the charges against him were vaguely worded; his assertion that he only used open sources were never verified; investigators based the charges on secret decrees that Sutiagin was not allowed to see; the FSB violated numerous rules of criminal procedure; and officials publicly denounced Sutiagin as a spy prior to and during his trial.<ref>{{cite web |title=Russia’s “Spy Mania”: A Study of the Case of Igor Sutiagin : CASE STUDY: IGOR SUTIAGIN |work=[[Human Rights Watch]] |url=https://www.hrw.org/legacy/backgrounder/eca/russia/4.htm}}</ref> Human rights activists argued that he had no access to secrets and had been working openly with academics.<ref name =profiles>{{cite news |title=Profile: Russian spies released |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/world/us_and_canada/10551319.stm |publisher=BBC |date=2010-07-09 |accessdate=2010-07-09}}</ref>

==US–Russia spy swap==
On 9 July 2010, Sutyagin along with [[Illegals Program#Prisoners held by Russia involved in the exchange|three other pardoned agents]] was released by Russia in exchange for the release of [[Illegals Program|10 people]] arrested in the United States of spying for Russia.<ref>{{cite news |first=Greg |last=White |title=Prisoner-Swap Deal Reported Likely in Russia Spy Case |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424052748704545004575352441951328652 |newspaper=[[The Wall Street Journal]] |date=2010-06-07 |accessdate=2010-06-07}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2010/jul/09/russian-spies-swap-us|title=Spy swap: US and Russia hand over agents in full media glare|first1=Tom|last1=Parfitt|first2=Matthew|last2=Weaver|first3=Richard|last3=Norton-Taylor|date=9 July 2010|website=the Guardian}}</ref> Sutyagin had always maintained his innocence but agreed to sign an admission of guilt as part of the deal.<ref name =release>{{cite news |first=Tom |last=Parfitt |title='Spy swap' begins as Russian scientist reportedly leaves Moscow |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2010/jul/08/russian-spy-swap-us |newspaper=[[The Guardian]] |date=2010-07-09 |accessdate=2010-07-09 | location=London}}</ref> Sutyagin reports that he had been asked to sign a pardon request falsely admitting guilt as early as 2005.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.rferl.org/a/Interview_Igor_Sutyagin_Discusses_Spy_Swap_Life_In_England/2127860.html|work=Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty|title=Interview: Igor Sutyagin Discusses 'Spy Swap,' Life In England|date=14 August 2010|author=Natalya Golitsyna|place=London}}</ref> Shortly after his release, he told [[RFE/RL]] in an interview in August 2010, he just had been working for money. ("They criticize me for earning money.")<ref>[https://www.rferl.org/a/Interview_Igor_Sutyagin_Discusses_Spy_Swap_Life_In_England/2127860.html Interview: Igor Sutyagin 'Spy Swap,' Life In England ], rferl,  14 August 2010</ref> Sutyagin hopes to rejoin his wife Irina Manannikova and daughters Oksana and Anastasiya.<ref name="NYT-20100813-topics">{{cite news|title=Times Topics: Igor Sutyagin|url=http://topics.nytimes.com/top/reference/timestopics/people/s/igor_v_sutyagin/index.html|work=[[New York Times]]|accessdate=17 August 2010|date=13 August 2010 | first=Peter | last=Baker}}</ref><ref name =release/> The US State Department does not consider Sutyagin to be a spy.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://2009-2017.state.gov/r/pa/prs/dpb/2010/07/144359.htm|title=We're sorry, that page can't be found.|website=www.state.gov}}</ref>

In 2011, [[European Court of Human Rights]] has found violations of Articles 5 and 6 of [[European Convention on Human Rights]] by Russian authorities in Sutyagin's case.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://cmiskp.echr.coe.int/tkp197/view.asp?action=html&documentId=884821&portal=hbkm&source=externalbydocnumber&table=F69A27FD8FB86142BF01C1166DEA398649|title=HUDOC - European Court of Human Rights|website=cmiskp.echr.coe.int}}</ref>
